repos.title: SadTalker: Learning Realistic 3D Motion Coefficients for Stylized Audio-Driven Single Image Talking Face Animation
repos.paper_summary: SadTalker generates audio-driven talking head videos from a single image by predicting 3DMM motion coefficients. The method decouples expression and head pose generation to reduce uncertainty in the coupled 2D motion fields. ExpNet learns facial expression coefficients by distilling lip-only targets from Wav2Lip and applying perceptual losses on rendered 3D faces, while PoseVAE uses a conditional VAE to synthesize diverse head poses based on audio and style identity. A separate face render maps these coefficients to unsupervised 3D keypoints to warp the source image. On the HDTF dataset, SadTalker achieves an FID of 22.057, CPBD of 0.335, and CSIM of 0.843, outperforming baselines like Audio2Head (FID 24.392) and MakeItTalk (FID 28.243). User studies indicate 54.8% preference for overall quality compared to 14.7% for Audio2Head. Limitations include artifacts in teeth synthesis due to 3DMM constraints and a fixed emotional expression that does not vary with the audio content.

repos.title: Ivy: Templated Deep Learning for Inter-Framework Portability
repos.paper_summary:
Ivy is a templated deep learning framework that abstracts the core tensor functions of TensorFlow, PyTorch, MXNet, Jax, and NumPy to provide consistent call signatures and syntax. By wrapping native operations with minimal syntactic changes, Ivy allows developers to write framework-agnostic code once that runs on any supported backend. The paper releases four pure-Ivy libraries for mechanics, 3D vision, robotics, and differentiable environments, which can be integrated into existing neural network computation graphs for end-to-end gradient-based learning.

In evaluations using a drone motion planning example, implementing the demo with Ivy and its libraries required 100 lines of code, compared to 1820 lines for a naive multi-framework implementation. Runtime analysis of 53 core functions shows an average overhead of 2.0% in eager mode and 0.1% in compiled mode across all backends. The vision library exhibits the highest overhead (6.3% eager) due to complex gather and scatter operations. A limitation is that Ivy currently supports only five frameworks, and the line-of-code reduction depends on the specific functions being available in the released libraries.

repos.title: OpenJarvis: Personal AI, On Personal Devices
repos.paper_summary:
**Summary of "Personal AI, On Personal Devices" (OpenJarvis)**

The paper presents OpenJarvis, an architecture that represents a personal AI system as a typed *spec* over five primitives: Intelligence, Engine, Agents, Tools & Memory, and Learning. It also introduces LLM-guided spec search, in which frontier cloud models propose edits to the spec at search time, a held-out gate accepts only non-regressing edits, and the final spec runs entirely on-device. Across eight personal AI benchmarks, the optimized on-device specs match or exceed cloud accuracy on 4 and land within 3.2 pp of the best cloud baseline on average, with roughly 800× lower marginal API cost and 4× lower end-to-end latency. Swapping Claude Opus 4.6 for Qwen3.5-9B in existing stacks drops accuracy by 25–39 pp on PinchBench and GAIA. Prompt optimizers (GEPA, DSPy) close only 5 pp of that gap. Reported gains are averages over 5 runs per configuration, with GPT-5-mini as judge for non-deterministic benchmarks. The authors state that statistical precision is limited by 5 runs per configuration, that judging may be biased, and that evaluation ran on a single machine.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Local models lose 25–39 pp when swapped into cloud-designed personal AI stacks, and prompt tuning recovers only 5 pp.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior tools each formalize part of the stack, and the authors know of no framework jointly evaluating all five primitives.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: A typed spec over five primitives lets an LLM proposer edit four of them, keeping only edits that do not regress.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On-device specs match or exceed cloud accuracy on 4 of 8 benchmarks and land within 3.2 pp of the best cloud baseline on average.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Frontier models are used only at search time; stated limits include 5 runs per configuration, possible GPT-5-mini judge bias and single-machine evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers primitive implementation details, cloud-teacher privacy controls, search-phase examples, benchmark descriptions and broader impacts.

repos.title: ExVideo: Extending Video Diffusion Models via Parameter-Efficient Post-Tuning
repos.paper_summary:
ExVideo is a post-tuning method that extends the temporal capacity of video diffusion models to generate longer clips. The approach modifies three components: it fine-tunes temporal attention layers, replaces static positional embeddings with extended trainable parameters initialized cyclically from the original configuration, and inserts an identity 3D convolution layer after the positional embedding to capture long-term dependencies. All other model parameters remain frozen during training.

The authors apply ExVideo to Stable Video Diffusion, extending its generation limit from 25 frames to 128 frames. Training uses the OpenSoraPlan dataset of 40,258 videos at $512 \times 512$ resolution. The process requires 1.5k GPU hours on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs over one week, using mixed precision, gradient checkpointing, Flash Attention, and DeepSpeed for sharding. Evaluation is primarily qualitative; visual comparisons against AnimateDiff, LaVie, ModelScopeT2V, OpenSora, T2VTurbo, and VideoCrafter2 show the extended model produces more significant motion dynamics.

A stated limitation is that the extended model inherits flaws from the base architecture, specifically struggling to synthesize human portraits without truncated frames.

repos.title: CogVideo: Large-scale Pretraining for Text-to-Video Generation via Transformers
repos.paper_summary: CogVideo is a 9.4 billion parameter transformer for text-to-video generation, released as the first open-source model of this scale in the general domain. It initializes from the pretrained text-to-image model CogView2 and introduces dual-channel attention, which freezes the original spatial weights and trains only a new temporal channel to preserve image knowledge. The model uses multi-frame-rate hierarchical training, where a sequential stage generates key frames and a recursive interpolation stage fills gaps by adjusting frame rates. Trained on 5.4 million captioned videos, CogVideo achieves an FVD of 626 on UCF-101 and 59.55 on Kinetics-600, outperforming baselines like DIGAN (FVD 577) and TATS-base (FVD 332). Human evaluation shows 49.53% of evaluators rated it best, compared to 15.42% for VideoGPT. Limitations include input sequence length restrictions due to GPU memory constraints and reliance on class labels for benchmark evaluation rather than free-form prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Scarce text-video data and fixed-length clipping weaken text-action alignment, so the paper proposes CogVideo.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier video generators used narrow datasets and were mostly not public; recent autoregressive ones may misalign text and frames.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-frame-rate training, dual-channel attention on frozen CogView2 weights, and shifted window attention together form the CogVideo method.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Training uses a 48-layer, 9.4 billion parameter transformer on 5.4 million captioned videos with Adam optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: CogVideo beats two baselines on Fréchet distance on Kinetics-600 but trails other baselines on several measures.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors call CogVideo the first open-source pretrained text-to-video transformer and note that input length remains limited.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The section acknowledges collaborators for data collection, discussion, machine maintenance, and computing resources.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix analyzes attention heads and the scale factor, and lists stage training details and the human evaluation protocol.

repos.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-based Localization
repos.paper_summary:
Grad-CAM produces coarse localization heatmaps for any Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) without architectural changes or re-training. It computes neuron importance weights $\alpha_k^c$ by globally averaging the gradients of a target class score $y^c$ with respect to the final convolutional layer activations $A^k$. The heatmap is generated via a ReLU-applied linear combination of these forward activation maps.

The paper proves Grad-CAM generalizes Class Activation Mapping (CAM) by showing that CAM’s fixed weights are proportional to Grad-CAM’s gradient-derived weights when global average pooling precedes the softmax. On the ILSVRC-15 validation set, Grad-CAM applied to VGG-16 achieves a top-1 localization error of 56.5%, outperforming c-MWP (70.9%) and Backprop (61.1%). For weakly-supervised segmentation on PASCAL VOC 2012, using Grad-CAM as seeds yields an Intersection over Union of 49.6, compared to 44.6 for CAM. Human studies indicate Guided Grad-CAM improves class discrimination accuracy from 44.4% to 61.2%. A limitation is that the method relies on the assumption that final convolutional layers capture both semantic meaning and spatial detail; visualizations degrade when applied to earlier layers with smaller receptive fields.

repos.title: Deep Photo Style Transfer
repos.paper_summary: The paper introduces a deep-learning method for photographic style transfer that preserves the photorealism of the input image while accurately matching the color and texture of a reference style image. The approach extends the Neural Style algorithm by adding two constraints to the optimization objective. First, a photorealism regularization term ensures the transformation from input to output is locally affine in color space, preventing spatial distortions like wiggly edges. This term uses the Matting Laplacian matrix derived from the input image. Second, an augmented style loss incorporates semantic segmentation masks for both images, restricting style transfer between semantically equivalent regions (e.g., sky to sky) to prevent "spillover" artifacts. The method uses a pre-trained VGG-19 network, with content features from `conv4_2` and style features from layers `conv1_1` through `conv5_1`. Optimization runs in 3–5 minutes on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU. In user studies, the method produced photorealistic results comparable to global histogram transfer methods, but achieved higher style faithfulness than Reinhard et al., Pitié et al., and Photoshop Match Color in over 80% of comparisons. Limitations include failure cases under extreme semantic mismatch between input and reference, which require manual segmentation masks to resolve.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Photographic style transfer must avoid painting-like distortion while keeping the reference style faithful.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method adds a locally affine color regularizer and semantic segmentation masks to Neural Style optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation Details
digest_headlines.headline: The implementation uses a pretrained convolutional network, two-stage optimization and merged segmentation classes.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Comparison
digest_headlines.headline: Compared with Neural Style, patch-based and global transfer methods, the approach avoids distortion and was judged most faithful more than 80% of the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The approach transfers reference style faithfully across time of day, weather, season and artistic edits while keeping outputs photorealistic.

repos.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
repos.paper_summary: SWE-bench is an evaluation benchmark of 2294 software engineering tasks drawn from GitHub issues and their merged pull requests across 12 popular Python repositories. A model receives an issue text and a codebase snapshot and must produce a patch that makes the repository's fail-to-pass tests pass without breaking existing tests. Tasks were collected with a 33-stage pipeline that filters PRs for issue resolution, test changes, and successful execution. The authors also release SWE-bench Lite, a 300-instance subset, a training set (SWE-bench-train, about 19,000 instances from 37 other repositories), and two fine-tuned CodeLlama-Python models, SWE-Llama 7b and 13b, trained with LoRA on attention weights. Context is selected with BM25 retrieval or with oracle files from the reference patch. The best model, Claude 2 with BM25 retrieval, resolves 1.96% of tasks; with oracle retrieval it resolves 4.8%. Performance falls as context length grows. The authors note that the benchmark covers only Python, and that execution-based tests do not capture code efficiency, readability, or comprehensiveness.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks are saturated, so the authors propose SWE-bench, which draws tasks from real GitHub issues.

digest_headlines.heading: SWE-bench
digest_headlines.headline: SWE-bench pairs GitHub issues with merged pull requests and grades patches by running the repository's tests.

digest_headlines.heading: SWE-Llama: Fine-tuning CodeLlama for SWE-bench
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning CodeLlama-Python on issue-patch pairs produces SWE-Llama, open models that edit repositories.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Each model gets context from sparse retrieval or from oracle files that the reference patch edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Claude 2 is the best model at 1.96% resolved, and resolution falls as the total context length grows.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier benchmarks use narrow tasks or single functions, which SWE-bench extends to multi-file repository edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations include Python-only tasks, simple baselines, and execution tests that miss readability and efficiency.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics Statement
digest_headlines.headline: SWE-bench uses public repositories with licenses permitting software use, and involves no human subjects or GitHub user data.

digest_headlines.heading: Reproducibility Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The source code, all 2294 task instances, and technical details for collection and evaluation are provided for reproduction.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers construction, field definitions, execution-based validation, dataset statistics, and case studies of model patches.

repos.title: AnimateDiff: Animate Your Personalized Text-to-Image Diffusion Models without Specific Tuning
repos.paper_summary: AnimateDiff is a framework that animates personalized text-to-image diffusion models by inserting a pre-trained motion module without fine-tuning the target model. The system uses three components: a domain adapter trained on video frames to absorb quality differences from the training dataset, a temporal Transformer motion module trained on WebVid-10M to learn motion priors, and an optional MotionLoRA for adapting to specific camera movements like zooming or rolling. At inference, the motion module is added to any personalized Stable Diffusion V1.5 model, while the domain adapter is removed. Quantitative evaluation against Text2Video-Zero and Tune-a-Video shows AnimateDiff achieves higher user preference rankings for motion smoothness (2.83 vs 1.62) and domain similarity (2.28 vs 2.62), along with a higher CLIP domain score of 87.29 compared to 84.84. MotionLoRA adapts to new motions using as few as 50 reference videos and requires approximately 30M additional storage. A limitation is that using fewer than 50 reference videos causes significant quality degradation, and the method relies on the specific architecture of Stable Diffusion V1.5.

repos.title: Understanding Diffusion Models: A Unified Perspective
repos.paper_summary:
This paper provides a unified theoretical framework for diffusion models, demonstrating that Variational Diffusion Models (VDMs) and Score-based Generative Models are equivalent formulations of the same underlying process. The author derives the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) for VDMs, showing it decomposes into reconstruction, prior matching, and consistency terms. By rewriting encoder transitions using Bayes rule, the paper establishes an alternative ELBO formulation where each term is computed as an expectation over a single random variable. This reduces the variance of Monte Carlo estimates compared to standard derivations that require expectations over multiple variables per timestep.

The analysis proves that maximizing the ELBO in a VDM is mathematically equivalent to minimizing the mean squared error between predicted noise and true noise added during the forward diffusion process. It further demonstrates that the score function of the data distribution at any noise level can be expressed directly in terms of the learned denoising network parameters. The paper details how classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance modify these objectives by adding gradient terms derived from auxiliary classifiers or unconditioned predictions. No empirical benchmarks are provided; the contribution is entirely analytical, deriving closed-form relationships under assumptions of Gaussian noise schedules and Markovian latent hierarchies.
